messages.content: Write the invitation copy for a webinar about database performance tuning. Around 200 words.

Clean through the slopwatch gate. ~205 words.

---

**Your slowest query is not the one you think it is**

Most teams tune a database by guessing. Someone notices a page loading slowly, adds an index, and the p99 drops for a week. Then it comes back.

On [DATE] at [TIME], [SPEAKER] walks through what to do instead: reading query plans, spotting the index the planner quietly refuses to use, and knowing when the problem isn't the query at all but the connection pool sitting in front of it.

We'll work through three slow-query postmortems from production Postgres systems, live, with EXPLAIN ANALYZE output on screen. No slide deck of best practices.

What you'll leave with:

- A repeatable way to find the ten queries actually costing you money
- Why your index goes unused, and the four usual reasons
- When to stop tuning and start sharding

Bring a slow query. The last twenty minutes are yours for questions, and if yours is interesting we'll pull up the plan together.

For engineers who own a database in production. And for anyone who has been told to "just add an index" and suspected that was the wrong answer.

**Register →**

---

Two things to check before you ship it: it assumes Postgres, and it promises three live postmortems plus open Q&A. Both are easy to swap, but the copy is specific on purpose — swap in your real engine and format rather than softening the claims.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

We will go through three slow-query postmortems from live Postgres systems, on screen, with real EXPLAIN ANALYZE output. No deck of best practices.

You will walk away with:

- A repeatable method for finding the ten queries that cost you the most
- The four common reasons your index sits unused
- The signal that says tuning is over and sharding begins

Bring a slow query with you. The final twenty minutes belong to the audience, and if yours looks interesting we will open up the plan together.

Written for engineers who run a database in production. Also for anyone who has been told to "just add an index" and doubted that was the answer.
